prompt: Ana runs `GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build .` in `~/cross`, with no `-o`. What appears in the directory?
hint: Look at the `ls` that followed the four builds.

choices.text: Nothing: a Windows binary has to be built on Windows
choices.why: The build succeeded on Linux and `file` read the result as a Windows executable. No Windows machine was involved.

choices.text: `hits.exe`, a PE32+ executable for x86-64
choices.why: Right. Without `-o` the go command names the output after the module and adds `.exe` because the target is Windows.

choices.text: A file called `hits` that overwrites the Linux binary
choices.why: The native `hits` was still there in the `ls`. The `.exe` is added for a Windows target when the go command picks the name itself.

choices.text: `hits-windows-amd64`, named after the two variables
choices.why: That is the name `release.sh` chooses in section 05. `go build` on its own only adds the extension.

prompt: Building `hits` for `linux/arm64` on an Intel laptop needed no ARM compiler and no ARM C library. Why?
hint: Two halves: what builds the binary, and what the binary needs when it runs.

choices.text: The go command downloads an ARM toolchain from the module proxy the first time
choices.why: Nothing was downloaded; the build works with no network. The compiler for every target is the one already in `/usr/local/go`.

choices.text: The binary is bytecode that a small runtime interprets on any processor
choices.why: `file` read it as ARM aarch64 machine code, and the kernel of this Intel machine refused to run it. Go compiles to native instructions.

choices.text: The toolchain and standard library are Go, and Linux binaries skip libc
choices.why: Right. The standard library is compiled for `arm64` into the build cache, and the result is `statically linked` because it makes its system calls itself.

choices.text: Ubuntu's `gcc` already contains a back end for every processor Go supports
choices.why: Section 04 showed the host's `gcc` failing on ARM assembly. A cross build of a pure Go program does not call `gcc` at all.

prompt: How many `GOOS/GOARCH` pairs did `go tool dist list | wc -l` count for Go 1.27.1?
hint: One pair per line.

prompt: Match each target with what `file` said about the binary built for it.
hint: The format names the system; the processor follows it.

pairs.right: Mach-O 64-bit arm64, flags DYLDLINK and PIE

prompt: `./hits-arm64 count access.log` ends in `Exec format error` and exit status 126 on Ana's Intel machine. What does that say?
hint: Compare it with lesson 1's 127.

choices.text: The kernel found the file and cannot load its format
choices.why: Right. 126 means found and not executable; the header names a processor this kernel does not drive.

choices.text: The build was corrupted and must be redone
choices.why: The same file ran under `qemu-aarch64-static` and printed lesson 1's table to the digit.

choices.text: The file lacks execute permission
choices.why: Permission denied is a different message. `go build` makes the output executable.

choices.text: The shell could not find `./hits-arm64` in the directory
choices.why: Not found is 127, as in lesson 1. Here the file was found.

prompt: Somebody hands you a binary called `hits` and asks which machine it is for. Which command answers, including whether cgo was on, without running it?
hint: One command read `GOOS`, `GOARCH` and `CGO_ENABLED` out of `hits-arm64`.

choices.text: `go env GOOS GOARCH`
choices.why: That prints the settings of the go command on this machine, not the ones a binary was built with.

choices.text: `go version -m hits`
choices.why: Right. It reads the build record inside the binary: the Go release, `GOOS`, `GOARCH`, `CGO_ENABLED` and the level such as `GOARM64=v8.0`.

choices.text: `qemu-aarch64-static ./hits -h`
choices.why: That runs it, and only works if it is an ARM binary; it prints the usage, not the build settings.

choices.text: `file hits | cut -d, -f1,2`
choices.why: `file` gives the format and the processor, but knows nothing of `CGO_ENABLED`.

prompt: `GOARCH=arm64 go test -count=1 ___ qemu-aarch64-static .` builds an ARM test binary and runs it through the emulator.
hint: The `go test` flag that names a program to run the test binary through.

prompt: A project starts shipping a `linux/riscv64` build, and you have no RISC-V machine. How do you run its tests on that processor from your Intel laptop?
hint: The lesson did this for one processor; the emulator package has one program per processor.

choices.text: `GOARCH=riscv64 go test -exec qemu-riscv64-static .`
choices.why: Right. Same shape as the `arm64` run: the go command builds a RISC-V test binary and `-exec` hands it to QEMU's emulator for that processor.

choices.text: `go test .`, since a test passing on amd64 passes on every processor
choices.why: Lesson 1's test happens to pass on both, but that is what running it on the other processor shows, not something the native run proves.

choices.text: `GOARCH=riscv64 go test .`, which emulates the target automatically
choices.why: With `GOARCH=arm64` and no `-exec`, the same command failed with `exec format error`. Nothing is emulated unless you ask.

choices.text: `qemu-riscv64-static go test .`
choices.why: That would try to run the Intel `go` binary on an emulated RISC-V processor. The emulator has to run the test binary, not the go command.

prompt: On a machine with `gcc` installed, `go env CGO_ENABLED` prints `1` and `GOARCH=arm64 go env CGO_ENABLED` prints `0`. Why the difference?
hint: Which processor does the installed `gcc` produce code for?

choices.text: Cross builds turn cgo off: the host's `gcc` makes host code
choices.why: Right. The cgo documentation says it is disabled by default when cross-compiling; a C compiler for the target has to be named in `CC`.

choices.text: ARM processors have no way to call C code, so cgo means nothing there
choices.why: `go tool dist list -json` marks most ports, ARM ones included, as `CgoSupported`. What is missing here is a C compiler for ARM.

choices.text: Setting `GOARCH` took `gcc` off the `PATH` for that one command
choices.why: `GOARCH` changes nothing about `PATH`. Lesson 1's missing-`gcc` case is a different cause with the same symptom.

choices.text: Go 1.27.1 removed cgo support for `arm64`
choices.why: It was not removed; with a cross C compiler in `CC` and `CGO_ENABLED=1` it builds.

prompt: The native `who` came out `dynamically linked` and the `arm64` one `statically linked`, from the same source. What made the difference?
hint: `go list -f '{{.CgoFiles}}' os/user` answered differently for the two targets.

choices.text: The ARM linker cannot write a dynamically linked executable
choices.why: The macOS build was dynamically linked against `libSystem` from this very machine. The difference here is which files of `os/user` were compiled.

choices.text: `os/user` compiled its cgo files natively and pure Go for ARM
choices.why: Right. With cgo on it calls the C library's account functions; with cgo off it reads `/etc/passwd` and `/etc/group` itself.

choices.text: `qemu-aarch64-static` linked the C library into the binary as it ran it
choices.why: `file` read the binary before any emulator touched it. QEMU runs a binary; it does not change it.

choices.text: `user.Current` returns a different user on ARM
choices.why: Both printed `ana /home/ana`. The answer was the same; the way of getting it differed.

prompt: `GOARCH=arm64 go build` of `twice`, whose `main.go` has `import "C"`, fails with `build constraints exclude all Go files`. What happened?
hint: A file that imports "C" carries an implied condition.

choices.text: With cgo off the file was left out, and no file remained
choices.why: Right. `import "C"` implies the `cgo` build constraint; cgo is off for a cross build, so `main.go` was excluded and the package had nothing to compile.

choices.text: `twice/main.go` has a syntax error that only ARM's parser notices
choices.why: The native build compiled it and printed 42. The parser is the same for every target.

choices.text: The module needs a `//go:build arm64` line before it can target ARM
choices.why: `hits` has no such line and built for every target. No file needs to declare a processor to be compiled for it.

choices.text: `gcc` refused the C function in the comment
choices.why: That is what happened with `CGO_ENABLED=1`, and the message was about assembler instructions. With cgo off `gcc` is never called.

prompt: A team builds its agent with `GOAMD64=v3` because a benchmark on their laptops was faster. One customer runs it on servers with Intel processors from 2009. What do those servers see?
hint: The emulated Nehalem is a 2008 design.

choices.text: The program runs, a little slower, using the v1 instructions instead
choices.why: There is no v1 path inside a v3 binary. The emulated Nehalem got a refusal, not a slower run.

choices.text: A refusal naming v3, exit 1, before `main`
choices.why: Right. The runtime checks the processor at start-up; `hits-v3` printed exactly that under `-cpu Nehalem` and exited 1.

choices.text: The kernel refuses it with `Exec format error`
choices.why: The format is the same ELF for x86-64; the kernel loads it. It is Go's runtime that refuses, with its own message.

choices.text: A crash with an illegal instruction partway through the run
choices.why: That is what the start-up check exists to prevent: the refusal comes before any v3 instruction runs.

prompt: Which of these can change between two builds of the same package that differ only in `GOOS` and `GOARCH`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of cgo, file selection and what the binary records.

choices.text: Whether cgo is used, by default
choices.why: Yes. Native builds default to `CGO_ENABLED=1` where a compiler exists; cross builds default to `0`.

choices.text: Which source files of a package are compiled
choices.why: Yes. `os/user` compiled its cgo files for one target and none for the other, and files named for one system are skipped on the rest.

choices.text: The module path written in `go.mod`
choices.why: `go version -m` showed `example.com/hits` for the ARM build, as for every other. The module is the source, not the target.

choices.text: What `hits count access.log` prints
choices.why: The native and emulated runs printed the same table, and `diff` found no difference in `top -n 8`.

prompt: `release.sh` builds every target with `CGO_ENABLED=0`, even `linux/amd64`, the machine it runs on. What does that buy?
hint: Compare the `CGO_ENABLED` that `go version -m` read from the plain `hits` and from the release's `linux/amd64`.

choices.text: Faster builds
choices.why: Build speed is not the point; the cache makes the second release fast either way.

choices.text: All six built the same way
choices.why: Right. Left out, the native target would be built with cgo on and the other five with it off, and a program using `os/user` or `net` would behave differently on one system.

choices.text: It removes the debugging information from each binary
choices.why: The binaries still carry it; removing it is lesson 17's linker flags.

choices.text: It lets `hits` call C on the Windows targets
choices.why: `0` turns cgo off. `hits` calls no C anywhere.

prompt: Why does `release.sh` start with `rm -rf release` instead of building into whatever is already there?
hint: Think of a target that was on the list last month and is not now.

choices.text: `go build -o` refuses to overwrite an existing file
choices.why: `go build -o` overwrites happily; the native `hits` was rebuilt in place more than once.

choices.text: A binary for a target dropped from the list would linger and ship
choices.why: Right. Building into an old directory replaces what is on the list and leaves everything else, including binaries nobody built this time.

choices.text: It clears the build cache so every binary is compiled from scratch
choices.why: The build cache is in `~/.cache/go-build`, not in `release/`, and the script relies on it to make a second run fast.

choices.text: `set -eu` fails on a directory that already exists
choices.why: `set -eu` stops on a failing command or an unset variable. `mkdir release` would fail on an existing directory, which is why it runs after the `rm`, but the reason for the `rm` is the stale files.

prompt: Put in order what one pass of `release.sh`'s loop does for `windows/arm64`.
hint: From the word in the list to the line printed.
items: `ext` is set to `.exe`, because the system is Windows
the script prints the file's name

prompt: In the release directory, the largest binary was `hits-windows-amd64.exe` at 4,217,344 bytes and the smallest `hits-linux-arm64` at 3,831,466. How many bytes apart are they?
hint: Subtract.

prompt: A user asks for `hits` on a first-generation Raspberry Pi running 32-bit Linux. You add `linux/arm` to `release.sh`'s list and change nothing else. What is wrong with the binary it makes?
hint: What does `GOARCH=arm go env GOARM` print on an Intel machine?

choices.text: Nothing; `GOARCH=arm` runs on every ARM board
choices.why: `arm` covers several generations, and the default for a cross build is the newest of them.

choices.text: It is built for ARMv7, and that Pi's ARMv6 processor lacks instructions ARMv7 code uses
choices.why: Right. A cross build to `arm` defaults to `GOARM=7`; that board needs `GOARM=6`, which the loop would have to set for that one target.

choices.text: It is a 64-bit binary that a 32-bit system cannot load
choices.why: `GOARCH=arm` is 32-bit; `file` read the `GOARM=6` build as ELF 32-bit. 64-bit ARM is `arm64`.

choices.text: It needs `CGO_ENABLED=1` to run on a Raspberry Pi
choices.why: `hits` calls no C, and the `GOARM=6` build ran under `qemu-arm-static` with cgo off.

prompt: A teammate adds a feature to `hits` that calls a C library through cgo, and `release.sh` starts failing. Which target fails first, and why?
hint: The script builds the list in order, with `CGO_ENABLED=0` for every target.

choices.text: `windows/amd64`, because Windows has no C library
choices.why: Windows has C libraries. The failure comes before any system-specific question: cgo is off for every target in the script.

choices.text: Only the `arm64` targets, because they need an ARM `gcc`
choices.why: They would need one if cgo were on. With `CGO_ENABLED=0` the native target fails just the same.

choices.text: `linux/amd64`, the first, since cgo files are left out with cgo off
choices.why: Right. The files importing "C" are excluded for every target, so the first build already fails and `set -eu` stops the script there.

choices.text: None fail; the go command switches to a pure Go version of the library
choices.why: That happens for standard packages like `os/user`, which ship two implementations. A teammate's C library has no Go twin.

hint: The flag that changes the output to a machine-readable format.
